claims.text: The baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static yield strength of 786 MPa.
The baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
The baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static fracture strain of 13.5%.
Thermomechanical processing or controlled solidification can incorporate nanoscale precipitates of a ductile Nb- or V-containing phase into HfZrTiTa0.53.
The intervention will produce nanoscale ductile-phase precipitates within the alloy matrix.
The nanoscale precipitates will impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion will increase strain hardening.
The ductile nature of the precipitates will promote energy absorption.
The precipitates will delay shear-band formation.
Delayed shear-band formation will improve uniform deformability and resistance to localization.
The modified alloy will have approximately 10–20% greater yield strength than the baseline.
The modified alloy's fracture strain will increase by 5–10% relative to the baseline.
The modified alloy will exhibit less shear-band formation than the baseline.
The modified alloy will exhibit lower impact-induced energy release because failure is delayed.
The predictions apply under adiabatic dynamic deformation at strain rates from 10^3 to 10^5 s^-1.
Direct evidence for the effects of nanoscale precipitates in refractory high-entropy alloys under dynamic deformation is limited.
The outcome may depend on precipitate size, distribution, and phase compatibility.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome specifies lower impact-induced energy release, whereas the falsification rule asks for an unspecified 'improvement' in energy release; without defining improvement as a decrease, the directions are inconsistent or ambiguous.
